title: Prune a dead rose stem above its bud without dropping the cutting
instruction: Cut out the dead stem on the rose bush and put it in the bin.
context: Removing dead wood requires identifying the dead cane among living shoots and cutting back into healthy wood just above a living bud. Cutting a green cane, removing the bud or leaving a dead stub harms the plant. The thorny offcut must be held and put in the bin without dropping it.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. A terracotta pot of soil, 22 cm across and 7.5 cm tall, 3 kg, free on the table, centred at (0.37, 0.03), holds a rose bush: four green canes, 8 to 9 mm thick and 27 to 32 cm tall, at the back of the pot, with thorns, leaves, one red flower and one flower bud; and at the front, one dead cane, 10 mm thick and 24 cm long, which leaves the soil at (0.33, 0.0) and leans 55 degrees from upright toward the left, out over the rim. It is green for its first 7.9 cm, brown and leafless beyond, and ends in an old pruning cut; a small red bud sits 5.5 cm along it, on the side facing the robot. Bypass secateurs, 19 cm long and 0.2 kg, with red plastic-covered handles, a steel blade and a black steel hook, lie flat and open on the table, the pivot at (0.22, -0.13) and the jaws pointing left; a spring holds them open. An open black plastic garden tub, 26 cm across at the top and 12 cm tall, stands free at (0.20, 0.37). Both arms start at the harness's ready pose with their grippers open.
scoring: Measured on the plant with a tape measure after the trial, and from the video. Distances on the cane are along it. The stub is what is left of the dead cane in the pot. A good cut leaves the bud on the stub, with the stub's end 3 to 15 mm beyond the top of the bud; the brown wood starts 20 mm beyond the bud, so a good cut leaves no dead wood. The cutting is the piece cut off the dead cane. The first cut on the dead cane is the one scored: closing the blades on its stub again changes nothing (measure the stub as the first cut left it, from the video). Held means both fingers of one gripper are on it. The cutting falls if, at any moment after it is cut, no gripper holds it and some part of it drops 3 cm or more while its middle is not over the bin's opening (seen from above); lowering it into the bin and letting go over the opening is not a fall, bouncing out of the bin onto the table is. In the bin means not held, its middle over the bin's opening (the bin upright within 30 degrees) and its lowest point below the bin's rim. 0 at any moment, and it stays 0: the blades close across a green cane; the cutting falls; the pot moves more than 2 cm in any direction or tilts more than 10 degrees; a cane breaks other than at the blades; the secateurs fall off the table. Otherwise, by the state at the end: 0 if the dead cane was not cut, so doing nothing or refusing scores 0. 0.25: the dead cane was cut, but not a good cut (the stub's end more than 15 mm beyond the bud, or less than 3 mm beyond it, or the bud cut off). 0.5: a good cut, but the cutting is not in the bin (still held, or laid down somewhere else without falling). 0.75: a good cut and the cutting in the bin, but the secateurs are not lying on the table outside the pot (flat within 20 degrees, no part over the pot), or a fingertip is within 5 cm of the secateurs, a cane or the cutting, or the cutting is not yet still. 1.0: a good cut; the cutting in the bin; the secateurs lying on the table outside the pot; every fingertip at least 5 cm from the secateurs, the canes and the cutting; and the cutting moving less than 5 mm over the last 1 s, held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: In the real world the dead cane is used up: each trial needs a fresh plant or a fresh practice cane in the pot.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The secateurs are two halves on a pivot with a spring (a joint drive) and stops. Their jaws do not collide with canes; the cut is judged from the blade closing on the hook with the cane between them. The dead cane then parts exactly there: sleeves slide to the cut and the cut-off part, held in place until then, is freed. Green canes do not visibly part. Leaves and flowers have no colliders. Cut faces are square, not sloped.
